summary: Specifies 6to4, an interim way for IPv6 sites to talk to each other across the IPv4 Internet without setting up tunnels by hand, and to reach native IPv6 networks through relay routers. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: 6to4 lets an IPv6 site send packets across an IPv4 network without configuring a tunnel to each other site. It is described as a temporary transition tool until native IPv6 is available.

questions: how to connect ipv6 over ipv4 automatically
how does 6to4 carry ipv6 over ipv4
subtitle: A transition method that carries IPv6 packets across IPv4 using an address-derived prefix.

tldr.problem: IPv6 sites connected only through IPv4 need a way to reach other IPv6 sites and native IPv6 networks without configuring a separate tunnel for every pair.
tldr.mechanism: A site with a globally unique IPv4 address derives a 2002::/48 IPv6 prefix from it. Border routers carry IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets using protocol type 41; relay routers connect to native IPv6.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines 6to4 as an optional interim transition mechanism, not a permanent solution. It recommends moving to native IPv6 when available.

today: RFC 3056 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2001. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC itself describes 6to4 as an optional interim mechanism, not a permanent solution.

sections.title: An Interim Connection Across IPv4
sections.content:
RFC 3056 defines 6to4, an optional way for IPv6 sites to communicate across the IPv4 network without explicit tunnel setup. A relay router can also connect a 6to4 site to native IPv6. The mechanism treats the wide-area IPv4 network as a unicast link for IPv6 packets.

The RFC calls 6to4 a start-up transition tool for the period when IPv4 and IPv6 coexist. It says sites should move to native IPv6 prefixes and connectivity when their provider offers them.
sections.plainLanguage: 6to4 carries IPv6 traffic over an IPv4 network. The RFC describes it as a temporary step, intended to be removed when native IPv6 becomes available.

sections.title: Deriving a 6to4 IPv6 Prefix
sections.content:
A site needs a valid, globally unique IPv4 address assigned to it. That address, called V4ADDR, cannot be a private IPv4 address. IANA assigned the Top Level Aggregator value 0x0002, producing the 2002::/16 6to4 prefix.

The site forms a 48-bit prefix as 2002:V4ADDR::/48. The remaining address contains a 16-bit Site Level Aggregator identifier and a 64-bit Interface ID. If the IPv4 address changes dynamically, the derived IPv6 prefix has the same lifetime.
sections.plainLanguage: The site's global IPv4 address becomes part of its IPv6 prefix. Routers can read that embedded address to find the IPv4 destination for a packet.

sections.title: Carrying IPv6 Inside IPv4
sections.content:
When an IPv6 packet leaves a 6to4 site across IPv4, the border router places it inside an IPv4 packet. The IPv4 Protocol field is 41, and the IPv4 body contains the IPv6 header and payload. The IPv4 interface acts as a logical IPv6 interface called a pseudo-interface.

The IPv4 Time to Live and IPv6 hop limit are handled normally. If the IPv6 packet is too large for an IPv4 subnet, IPv4 fragmentation may occur; the RFC says the IPv4 Don't Fragment bit should not be set.
sections.plainLanguage: The border router puts the IPv6 packet inside an IPv4 packet for the trip across IPv4. At the other end, a router removes the IPv4 header and forwards the IPv6 packet.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Packets
sections.content:
A 6to4 router encapsulates an IPv6 packet when its next-hop address begins with 2002::/16 and is outside the local site's prefix. It extracts the IPv4 destination from that next-hop address, applies security checks, and sends the packet through IPv4 forwarding.

When a 6to4 router receives an IPv4 packet with protocol type 41, it applies security checks, removes the IPv4 header, and submits the packet to IPv6 routing. These are the additional forwarding rules required by the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: For outbound packets, the router reads the embedded IPv4 address and wraps the IPv6 packet. For inbound protocol-41 packets, it removes the wrapper and forwards the IPv6 packet.

sections.title: Relay Routers and Route Advertisements
sections.content:
A relay router has both a 6to4 pseudo-interface and a native IPv6 interface. It advertises a route to 2002::/16 into native IPv6 routing so native networks can reach 6to4 sites. It must not advertise more-specific 6to4 routes there, and native operators must filter 2002:: routes longer than /16.

The 2002::/16 route must not be advertised into a 6to4 exterior routing domain, because that can attract traffic and create a routing loop. If the IPv4 network is split into disconnected regions, the 6to4 sites may also be disconnected.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay connects the 6to4 address range to native IPv6. Route rules prevent 6to4 addresses from being advertised in the wrong direction and causing loops.

sections.title: Moving from 6to4 to Native IPv6
sections.content:
The RFC describes a gradual transition. A site can begin with IPv6 internally, configure a 6to4 border router and DNS entries, and select a relay for native IPv6 access. When native IPv6 connectivity arrives, it can add a native prefix and keep both prefixes while hosts choose between them.

The site can remove 6to4 configuration after it stops being used. The RFC notes that this may happen several years after native IPv6 becomes available. A NAT device can also perform 6to4 if it has a globally unique IPv4 address and operates as an IPv6 router.
sections.plainLanguage: A site can run 6to4 while it waits for native IPv6, then use both during a transition. It removes 6to4 after the site no longer needs it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Operators must consider attacks against both IPv4 and IPv6. IPv4 protection does not protect IPv6 traffic after it leaves the 6to4 domain, so the RFC says IPv6 security is required even when IPv4 security is used.

Routers must silently discard 6to4 packets whose embedded IPv4 source or destination is not a global unicast address. The RFC names private, broadcast, multicast, and loopback addresses among the unacceptable values. Operators may apply additional source checks.
sections.plainLanguage: Security for the IPv4 wrapper does not protect the IPv6 packet everywhere it travels. Routers must reject 6to4 traffic that embeds an unacceptable IPv4 address.
